charter.decision: Select the least-privilege GitHub authentication model for Blogbot's local Windows publication broker.
charter.primaryQuestion: Should Blogbot retain a classic OAuth App device flow with repo scope or migrate to a repository-selected GitHub App user access token?
subQuestions: Can a GitHub App use device flow from a desktop application without shipping an app private key?
Can access be limited to a user-selected installation repository?
Which repository permissions cover Blogbot's current REST endpoint set?
How should token expiration and refresh be handled locally?
Which parts still require an external owner or account mutation?
charter.scope: GitHub.com, local Windows desktop architecture, current Blogbot GitHub REST adapter endpoints, official English-language GitHub documentation checked on 2026-09-03.
exclusions: Registering or changing a GitHub App or OAuth App
Accessing private repositories or account secrets

methods.approach: Bounded decision-support scan using official GitHub documentation plus a focused inventory of the current native broker and REST endpoint paths.
inclusionCriteria: Current official GitHub documentation directly describing OAuth scopes, GitHub App device flow, repository selection, token lifecycle, or permissions for an endpoint used by Blogbot
Current Blogbot source that defines authentication or GitHub REST calls
exclusionCriteria: Search snippets without a checked official documentation page
Community posts, vendor summaries, and undocumented assumptions
Server-to-server designs that require shipping a GitHub App private key in the desktop application

claims.statement: The classic OAuth repo scope grants broad read/write repository access beyond Blogbot's single selected publication repository.
claims.uncertainty: The current repository is public, but the same token could reach private repositories available to the authorizing user.

claims.statement: A GitHub App user access token can be obtained through device flow for a desktop application without embedding an app private key, and its effective access is the intersection of app and user permissions.
claims.uncertainty: Device flow must first be enabled on an externally registered GitHub App.

claims.statement: A GitHub App installation can be limited to explicitly selected repositories instead of every repository accessible to the user.
claims.uncertainty: An installation owner must select and maintain the repository access externally.

claims.statement: Blogbot's current endpoint inventory maps to Contents write, Pull requests write, Checks read, Actions write, Administration read, and Metadata read; no organization or account permissions are evidenced by the current adapter.
claims.uncertainty: The exact minimum must be confirmed against every live endpoint response and X-Accepted-GitHub-Permissions header in a disposable repository.

claims.statement: Expiring GitHub App user access tokens support refresh tokens, and a token created through device flow can be refreshed without shipping an app private credential.
claims.uncertainty: The local broker must atomically persist expiration metadata and rotated access/refresh material before this is production-safe.

claims.statement: Blogbot should migrate from classic repo-scoped OAuth to a repository-selected GitHub App user-to-server device flow before enabling real GitHub publication.
claims.uncertainty: The recommendation cannot become an operational decision until an owner registers the app, accepts the exact permissions, and authorizes disposable-repository validation.

findings: The existing broker's repo scope and X-OAuth-Scopes validation are specific to a classic OAuth App and are incompatible with the preferred GitHub App user-token contract.

The current device-code endpoints and user-mediated flow can be retained conceptually, but token parsing, repository-installation validation, permission validation, expiration, and refresh storage must change together.
The least-privilege permission baseline evidenced by the adapter is Metadata read, Contents write, Pull requests write, Checks read, Actions write, and Administration read.
No GitHub App private key, installation JWT, webhook endpoint, organization permission, or account permission is needed for the user-attributed local desktop design.
disagreements: An installation access token would be shorter-lived and app-attributed, but minting it requires app authentication material that must not be shipped in this local desktop product; a user access token preserves local-only architecture and user attribution.
limitations: No GitHub App is currently registered or installed, so live token shape and permission headers were not exercised.
The current main branch is unprotected and no GitHub environment exists, so the complete protected publication policy cannot yet be rehearsed.
The scan covers GitHub.com official documentation and the adapter's current REST paths, not future endpoints.
recommendations: Adopt GitHub App user access tokens through device flow and remove the classic repo scope request.
Require installation access to exactly the configured repository and validate the installation repository list before storing an authorized state.
Request only Metadata read, Contents write, Pull requests write, Checks read, Actions write, and Administration read; request no webhook, organization, or account permissions.
Keep expiring user tokens enabled and atomically rotate the DPAPI-protected access token, refresh token, and their expirations.
Keep real GitHub login and publication disabled until external app registration and disposable-repository acceptance are separately authorized.

gaps: A human owner must register the GitHub App, enable device flow, select the target repository, and accept the exact permission set.
A disposable repository must prove token refresh, revocation, repository removal, insufficient-permission failure, branch protection reads, PR merge, ref cleanup, and workflow dispatch.
The native implementation and migration from any existing classic OAuth authorization state remain to be designed and tested.
approvalGates: GitHub App registration or account configuration requires explicit approval.
Disposable-repository writes, device authorization, pull requests, merge, workflow dispatch, and ref deletion require explicit approval.
No commit, push, release, publish, or deploy is authorized by this report.
